issues.legal_issue: A revenue-record entry identifying a person as occupant does not, by itself, transfer title to immovable property.
material_facts: The property had been acquired and developed with joint-family funds.
A revenue entry first recorded the prior owner and was later changed to identify the claimant as occupant after statements were made to revenue officials.
No registered instrument of transfer was executed, and the entry described the claimant as an occupant.
issues.conclusion: The revenue entry did not establish that title had passed to the claimant; in the circumstances, it supported an inference about possession only.
issues.legal_principle: A mutation or occupancy entry is not itself a conveyance of title. The Court distinguished the presumptive evidentiary value attributed to revenue entries in Gangabai v. Fakirgowda Somaypagowda Desai and Desai Navinkant Kesarlal v. Prabhat Kabhai, holding that this entry, which recorded the claimant as occupant and was unsupported by a registered transfer, could support possession but not title.

predicates.title_dispute_over_immovable_property: The parties disputed who held title to immovable property.
predicates.revenue_entry_records_occupancy: A public revenue record identified a person as occupying the property.
predicates.no_registered_transfer: No registered instrument transferring the property to that person was executed.

issues.definition: When a title dispute concerns property and the record identifies someone only as occupant without a registered transfer, the entry does not convey title.

issues.legal_issue: Account-book entries do not reliably establish a disputed claim when their correctness is unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The books included income attributed to the disputed property and were produced by the family member managing the property.
The plaintiff acknowledged that he had written some books on the manager's instructions but did not vouch for their reliability.
The manager did not testify or otherwise prove the correctness of the entries, and supporting records in his possession were not produced.
The books were objected to when tendered in evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the account books as unreliable and did not rely on them to establish the family's claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act makes entries in regularly kept books of account relevant, but the Court held that the entries in these books were not reliable in the absence of evidence supporting their correctness and in light of the missing supporting records.

rule.if: accounting_dispute and account_entries_offered_as_proof and no_witness_vouches_for_correctness and supporting_records_withheld

predicates.accounting_dispute: The parties disputed what income or property the accounts recorded.
predicates.account_entries_offered_as_proof: A party relied on entries in account books to support its position.
predicates.no_witness_vouches_for_correctness: No witness accepted responsibility for the accuracy of the entries.
predicates.supporting_records_withheld: Relevant corroborating records in a party's possession were not produced.

issues.definition: In an accounting dispute, entries offered without a witness supporting their accuracy and without relevant withheld corroboration are insufficient to prove the claim.

issues.legal_issue: Possession of a landlord's interest in tenanted property may be exercised through tenants and an agent.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the property as owner-landlord, subject to tenants' occupation, rather than a claim to evict the tenants.
The tenants paid rent under receipts identifying the claimant as the owner, and the manager collected rent on the claimant's behalf.
After the manager repudiated the claimant's claim, the claimant removed him from management and continued to exercise control through family members.
issues.conclusion: The tenants' physical occupation did not prevent the claimant from possessing the landlord's interest through them, and the manager's possession while acting as her agent was attributable to her.
issues.legal_principle: For an interest in property that is susceptible to possession through tenants, the nature of possession depends on the property and the interest claimed; tenants' attornment and payment of rent to a claimant can establish effective possession. An agent's possession is the principal's possession, and an agent in a fiduciary relationship cannot treat that possession as his own. The Court relied on Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and on Uppalapati Veera Venkata Satyanarayanaraju v. Josyula Hanummamma, David Lyelly v. John Lawson Kennedy, Williams v. Pott, and Secretary of State for India v. Krishnamoni Gupta.

rule.if: claim_to_landlord_interest and tenants_occupy_property and tenants_attorn_to_claimant and rent_collected_for_claimant_through_agent

predicates.claim_to_landlord_interest: A party claimed the landlord's interest in property while accepting that tenants occupied it.
predicates.tenants_occupy_property: Tenants, rather than the competing owners, physically occupied the property.
predicates.tenants_attorn_to_claimant: The tenants recognized the claimant as landlord and paid rent to or for that claimant.
predicates.rent_collected_for_claimant_through_agen: An agent collected rent on the claimant's behalf.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks the landlord's interest in tenanted property, tenants recognize the claimant, and an agent collects rent for the claimant, their possession can count as the claimant's possession.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who exclusively and adversely possesses a landlord's interest for the required limitation period acquires title by prescription, defeating a partition claim to that property.
material_facts: The property had been acquired and developed with joint-family funds.
The claimant asserted ownership, and tenants paid rent under receipts describing the property as hers, including receipts issued by the family manager and the plaintiff.
The manager collected rent for the claimant until he repudiated her claim; she then removed him from management and remained in exclusive control through her husband and son.
The claimant's possession continued from the asserted transfer until the partition suit was filed, exceeding the period required for prescription.

The Court rejected the competing family's account books and agreement as unreliable evidence of its claim to the property, and found the claimant's evidence and the surrounding circumstances credible.
issues.conclusion: The claimant acquired title by adverse possession. The Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's decision concerning the property, restored the trial court's decision dismissing the partition claim to it, and set aside the related account decrees.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, adverse possession of an interest in immovable property depends on an intention to claim exclusive title, demonstrated through possession hostile to the true owner's claim and appropriate to the nature of the property. The Court found that the claimant possessed the landlord's interest through tenants and an agent, followed by her family's continued control, for more than the required limitation period.

rule.if: partition_suit and claimant_asserts_exclusive_hostile_title and tenants_pay_rent_for_claimant and possession_continues_through_agent_or_successors_for_required_period

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding seeks partition of property claimed to belong to a family.
predicates.claimant_asserts_exclusive_hostile_title: A claimant asserts exclusive ownership against the persons claiming the property for the family.
predicates.tenants_pay_rent_for_claimant: Tenants pay rent to or for the claimant under arrangements recognizing the claimant's ownership.
predicates.possession_continues_through_agent_or_su: The claimant's possession, exercised through an agent and then through successors, continues for longer than the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, a claimant who asserts exclusive hostile title and receives rent from recognizing tenants, while possession continues through an agent or successors for the required period, acquires title by adverse possession and defeats the partition claim.
